component.name: JulAIn Music Player
component.summary: Chat with your music: play, search and shape your own library

description.p: JulAIn Music Player indexes a music folder you already own and plays it through mpv. You search it, queue it, build playlists, rank tracks by measured psychoacoustics, read timed lyrics and change every setting by typing or speaking a sentence in English or German.

ul.li: Talk to the library: “play something chill for an hour”, “find the most aggressive songs”, “make a smart playlist of 90s metal”.
Measure every song: 35 audio features become twelve sound axes, five profile sets and eight sound families, and every ranking explains why a track ranks where it does.
Read and edit tags and cover art, back up the measured data once a day, and inspect the library's health.
Search lyrics transcribed locally with Whisper, and ask for songs “about the sea” instead of by title.
Play through mpv with media keys and MPRIS, endless mode and radio, and a queue that survives closing the window.

description.p: The offline intent parser is the default; an optional OpenAI-compatible planner can be configured in the window. Nothing leaves the machine unless you pick a remote model or ask for an online catalogue match. The player never deletes audio and journals every playlist write. The window runs on GTK/WebKit and falls back to a browser window.

screenshot.caption: The sound profile: twelve measured axes as a net diagram, one slider per axis
One search box for titles, playlists and sung lines

description.p: The release number is shown once: the chat greeting no longer repeats it beside "JulAIn Music Player", so the badge in the window's top left is the one place it appears. Asking for the version (or /version) still answers with the number and the file it was read from.

The Profile panel and the "Why these values" box lead with what the track needs — "This track has not been analysed yet, and no lyrics have been transcribed for it." — and keep the machine reason below it as a dimmed second line, so the panel no longer opens with "no profile for this track yet".
A track whose psychology profile exists but whose row in the selected view is missing now names that view instead of claiming it has no profile at all. Nothing in the library is rewritten.

The playing track now says what it still lacks: the now-playing strip prints "not analysed · no lyrics", the Profile panel shows a chip per gap and the Lyrics panel names the missing analysis and whether a local transcriber is installed.
One read-only per-track answer feeds the status poll, both panels and the chat, and says when a transcription belongs to an older version of the file. Nothing in the library is rewritten.

The cover in the now-playing strip no longer disappears without a reason: a missing tag reader (a Debian install without python3-mutagen) is reported instead of looking like a track without art, and the cover is also found for a queue the chat did not start.
The running release is visible in the window, in the API and in the chat, read from the one VERSION file that ships with the code.

The now-playing strip shows the cover art: the picture embedded in the file, else the album's cover file, else the note icon. The box used to keep a fixed icon and never asked for a picture, so a library full of covers looked like it had none. It is served from a new read-only endpoint and nothing in the library is rewritten.

Tracks now blend at the join instead of cutting: a short fade out and in, as a playback filter that never touches the audio file. Two settings in the Playback group switch it on or off and choose the length, the chat understands "turn the fading off" and "fade the songs out over 5 seconds", and switching it off restores the untouched sound.

A question about the player is answered as a question again: "can you play spc files?" or "do you support flac" used to be searched for as if it were a title. Every reply also says whether the offline planner or the configured language model answered, and an offline dead end is handed to the model instead of stopping at "Nothing matches".

The package now ships AppStream metadata, so GNOME Software and App Center show the player with its name, description, icon, screenshots and release history. The 48–512 px icon sizes are part of the package again.

A media-key test now says why it failed: an app window older than the page, a missing or unreachable server address, or no MPRIS player. A plain F5–F8 that still reaches the window although a global binding exists is logged and reported as “not grabbed”.

The global media keys reach the running player again: the bindings call a helper that finds the live server, the MPRIS player or the CLI instead of a fixed “music-cli”. A Test button shows the route that works and names a conflicting shortcut.
The GNOME global media-key bindings use bare F5–F8 instead of the accelerator string “<F5>”, which GNOME ignored. Existing entries are rewritten in place on the next install.

Global media keys become a setting: Settings → Playback installs and removes the four GNOME shortcuts in one click, leaves every other custom shortcut alone, and says plainly that a plain F5–F8 is focus-only until the bindings are installed.
